[Discussion] What are some of the games that are really hard to review?

Probably papers please, because the more you describe it the more boring it sounds. It was a fun game (over praised/hyped but still interesting) that had the gameplay of reading documents and stamping stuff.
Undertale is kinda the same if you really like Earthbound humor as wished games had more humor like that then you will like it.

Not a specific game, but I think artistic games are very hard to review. Games like Journey for example. People say it's amazing and wonderful and I was bored by it. Gaming is subjective and each reviewer is going to have a different opinion, but artistic games are going to have a far bigger fluctuation of opinions in my mind. There was another game I can't remember the name of but you play as a breath of wind. I'm pretty sure it's not From Dust. It wasn't a game like that. But what can you say about a game like that? It's exploring an artistic world and nothing else. Those games have value, sure, but whether they're good or not is a far more difficult choice to make than with games you can look at objectively and from a technical standpoint.

This is basically it. I've had a few games that I've bought of the 'artistic sense', including Journey. They're neat, but I often feel that they're trying to make out they're the only game that's done it before.

The Stanley Parable for example. I downloaded the demo, was impressed with the humour and how they handled it as a demo for the game, and not of the game, but I thought the actual game was shit. It was neat, but I didn't really 'get' the whole idea.

Journey was neat in its artistic style and minimalistic communication, but had nothing in the way of story etc, all very vague do you interpret it however.

Homefront, the shitty 2011 shooter no one likes, is something that I really enjoyed. Linear as shit, unrealistic plot, but bro - you don't know it like I do.

So a lot of it is player taste, really. I don't touch JRPGs, but whenever I see one I hear how good the story is, etc.

On a related note, people don't always catch on to artistic statements put into games, and have a more negitive opinion of the game than they would of had they gotten it. Fallout New Vegas is a good example, no one seemed to get the juxtposition of the situation presented in the game's Mohjave desert to that of the real world Middle East. It just seemed pretty blunt to me that the NCR represented the West, Ceaser's Legion represented Islamic terrorists, and Mr. House represented corrupt Middle Eastern dictators. But many people write off the plot as stupid, but I found it to be a great example of modern allegory.

If a person is aiming to review games and share their findings with others, one of the first things they'll want to do is learn to delineate between whether or not a game is 'good', and whether or not they enjoyed playing it. A "good" game is a far more objective label than you might think.

There are plenty of very good games out there that I do not personally play or want to play because I don't enjoy games of that type. If I can say to readers/listeners/viewers that the game is solid all around and would very much appeal to <audience> even though I didn't particularly enjoy it myself, that speaks to a lot more objectivity and credibility than trying to make lame excuses for why the game wasn't good and therefore I didn't enjoy it.

Rank amateurs talk about flaws and try to shape their review to reflect their own subjective opinions Good reviewers know the difference between objective metrics and subjective interpretation.

Rust and DayZ fit the bill.

They're both completely player/server controlled environments. One reviewer can spend an entire day just wandering around by themselves until they're shot by a sniper.

Another can enter into an all out deathmatch, while another finds a survival situation where people get together and create little communities that defend themselves from bandits and PvE threats.

I find that a game such as Minecraft is extremely difficult to review completely because of the bazillion crazy things you can potentially do in multiplayer (and even singleplayer to an extent) with modded servers and such.
